text: In Bulgaria, as part of the EU, Bulgarian people, including mothers, performers, and government officials, express personal and emotional attachment, often through singing and speaking English, while also maintaining their cultural identity. This behavior aims to convey feelings, effectively communicate, and preserve their cultural heritage. Recipients, including Russians, foreign students, and the European Union, are expected to accept Bulgaria as a member, understand English, and may hold divided opinions due to differing memories of the communist era and the subsequent economic crisis. This behavior is perceived as relatively common within the sampled population, despite the division caused by historical and economic factors.

In Bulgaria and abroad, Bulgarians are known for their hardworking, friendly, and community-oriented behaviors, which aim to create a welcoming environment, improve living conditions, and earn a living. This is evident through their involvement in startups, maintenance of open borders, and active participation in social activities. Additionally, their unique food culture, including taco bread, fresh vegetables, and the use of garlic and rakia for health benefits, contributes to their distinct cultural identity. This mix of behaviors and cultural elements is widely regarded as normative within the sampled population, showcasing a significant level of acceptance and recognition. Foreign recipients, including tourists, Greeks, and foreign employers, often choose to engage in social activities and opt to stay in Bulgaria, indicating a positive reception of Bulgarian cultural practices.

In Bulgarian naming and language practices, Bulgarian individuals utilize a complex naming system that encompasses personal, patrilineal, and family names, along with gendered suffixes and variations based on family lineage and the status of unknown or unrecognized parents. This intricate naming convention serves the goal of identifying and distinguishing individuals and their family lineage. The broader society is expected to recognize and comprehend this naming system, reflecting a normative practice within the sampled population. This naming tradition is widely regarded as a standard and prevalent aspect of Bulgarian cultural identity, showcasing the significance placed on familial heritage and individual identification within Bulgarian society.

In Bulgarian social interaction, it is customary for Bulgarian individuals to use head movements to express agreement or disagreement, contrary to common global conventions. This behavior aims to facilitate effective communication within interpersonal relationships, whether with other Bulgarians or foreigners. Interestingly, the interpretation of these head movements differs from the global norm, as nodding up and down indicates 'no', while shaking side to side indicates 'yes'. This practice is widely regarded as the standard way of expressing agreement or disagreement within the Bulgarian cultural context, with around nine out of ten individuals in the sampled population adhering to this behavior.

Bulgarian individuals and the community living and working in the UK are commonly observed seeking a better life while preserving their cultural identity. This behavior involves experiencing culture shock, building relationships, and interacting with British people and society. Their goal is to express their identity, create a better world, and adapt to the new environment. This cultural behavior is influenced by the context of globalization and living abroad, reflecting the Bulgarian culture and identity. Within the sampled population, this behavior is widely regarded as normative, indicating that the majority of Bulgarians in the UK engage in these activities as they navigate their lives in a new cultural setting.

In various social and cultural settings, Bulgarians engage in celebratory practices, hospitality, and the consumption of traditional foods such as baked goods, sausages, and sandwiches. These practices serve the goals of expressing hospitality, celebrating holidays, and satisfying hunger. Partners, guests, and family members are the recipients of this hospitality and are expected to accept it and participate in the celebrations. There is a strong emphasis on traditional Orthodox celebrations and specific Bulgarian cuisine within these social and familial interactions. This behavior is widely regarded as a normative and standard practice within the Bulgarian cultural context, with a significant portion of the sampled population agreeing that it is a common and expected way of socializing and celebrating.

In the realm of Bulgarian television and online entertainment, Bulgarian people, YouTubers, and Twitch streamers engage in diverse forms of entertainment, such as watching Russian movies, cartoons, and American talk shows, while also aspiring to become content creators themselves. The goal behind this behavior encompasses entertainment, education, and financial success. The Bulgarian audience and learners reciprocate by consuming content that explores both Bulgarian and American culture. This cultural exchange takes place within the context of the post-communist regime, where the popularity of Russian cartoons and the influence of cultural representation play significant roles. This behavior is regarded as relatively common among the sampled population, reflecting a notable level of acceptance and participation within the Bulgarian cultural context.

In Bulgaria, particularly in resorts and camping areas, Bulgarians take on the role of hosts, creating visually appealing resorts with vibrant nightlife and engaging in outdoor activities such as camping and fishing. The goal is to attract tourists and provide entertainment for newcomers. Tourists and newcomers, in turn, visit and enjoy the resorts and nightlife, while seeking advice on camping from the locals. The Bulgarian camping culture also includes a focus on fishing and participation in local language forums. This behavior is regarded as moderately common among the sampled population, indicating that a significant portion of Bulgarians engage in these activities, particularly in resort and camping settings.

In various settings such as homes and kitchens, Bulgarian individuals, particularly mothers and parents, engage in the traditional preparation and consumption of Bulgarian food. This includes activities such as teaching, eating, and introducing dishes like tarator soup, Kashkaval cheese, and mekitsa to their children. The goal of this behavior is to pass down traditional recipes and familiarize children with Bulgarian cuisine. Children, in turn, learn and adopt these eating habits as part of the parent-child relationship and food preparation customs. This practice is widely regarded as a normative and standard way of preserving Bulgarian culinary heritage within the sampled population.

In Bulgarian literature and reading culture, Bulgarian authors and readers actively engage in creating, translating, and consuming a diverse range of literary works, encompassing surrealist and fantasy genres tailored for both children and adults. The primary goal of these literary endeavors is to express, entertain, educate, and convey meaningful messages to Bulgarian readers and international audiences. This literary landscape is influenced by a blend of traditional and modern styles, and the accessibility of Bulgarian literature is enhanced through translated works. This multifaceted engagement with literature is widely regarded as a normative and standard practice within the sampled population, reflecting a strong cultural emphasis on literary creation, consumption, and interpretation.

In Sofia, Bulgaria, both residents and taxi drivers are known to employ various strategies to safeguard valuables and facilitate financial transactions, aiming to ensure safety and ease of financial dealings for clients and businesses. This behavior is influenced by concerns about theft and a sense of paranoia, reflecting the prevalent need for security in such interactions. Additionally, the reciprocal behavior of providing assistance and services by the recipients further emphasizes the importance of these protective strategies. This approach is regarded as a common practice among a significant portion of the sampled population, indicating that it is widely accepted within the cultural context of Sofia, Bulgaria.

In various interpersonal relationships among Bulgarian speakers, it is customary to use unique and culturally specific terms of endearment such as 'mum', 'treasure', and 'sun' when addressing loved ones, family, and friends. The goal of this behavior is to express affection, and it is widely accepted by the recipients within these relationships. This practice is considered a normative and standard way of expressing love and closeness within the Bulgarian cultural context, with a significant portion of the sampled population agreeing that it is a common and expected behavior.

In various social and political settings within the Bulgarian cultural group, Bulgarian individuals, including leaders and citizens, commonly express appreciation, greet, and engage in conversation in Bulgarian as a way to show respect and socialize. This behavior extends to interactions with various recipients, including citizens and British people, encompassing both political and social contexts. Recipients typically respond to these greetings and participate in conversations. Additionally, there is a notable shift in address from "Bulgarian brethren" to "Dear citizens of the Republic of Bulgaria," reflecting changes in language usage over time. This behavior is regarded as moderately common within the sampled population, indicating that a significant portion of the group engages in these interactions as a customary practice.

In Bulgaria, Bulgarians interact with Macedonians with a sense of distinctiveness while respecting their right to live in their own country. This behavior is driven by the goal of promoting ethnic unity and respecting nationality, acknowledging the distinct cultural identity of Macedonians within Bulgaria. Macedonians, in turn, aspire for independence, reflecting their desire for autonomy and self-governance. The cultural perception in Bulgaria acknowledges the uniqueness of Macedonian culture and its separation from Bulgarian culture. This behavior is regarded as moderately normative within the sampled population, indicating that a significant portion of the population acknowledges and respects the distinctiveness of Macedonian culture while upholding the value of ethnic unity and national respect.

In the context of Bulgarian college and university students, it is customary for Bulgarian students to diligently engage in academic studies while simultaneously working to financially support themselves. The goal of this behavior is to acquire knowledge and ensure self-sufficiency. In return, the Bulgarian Literature Department and the students themselves take on the roles of educators and providers of financial support. This practice is influenced by the affordability of tuition and the value placed on self-reliance within the Bulgarian cultural setting. The sampled population widely regards this behavior as the standard and normative approach among Bulgarian college and university students.

In Bulgaria and interactions with British Bulgarians, people commonly engage in experiencing and navigating cultural differences. This includes aspects such as tipping practices, sharing experiences, visiting, expressing disagreement, speaking, and reacting to cultural disparities. The interactions may lead to culture shock, and it is important to consider the perspective of British Bulgarians in these situations. This behavior is widely regarded as normative within the sampled population, indicating that a significant portion of the population finds it common to actively engage with and adapt to cultural differences, particularly in the context of interactions with British Bulgarians.

In Bulgaria, people are known to adapt to diverse weather conditions, including both cold and hot temperatures, and they generally prefer using the Celsius temperature scale. The weather in Bulgaria is somewhat similar to Greece but slightly better, characterized by distinct four seasons and a sea temperature of 31 degrees. The preference for Celsius and the ability to adapt to varying weather conditions is widely regarded as a normative behavior within the sampled population.

In Bulgaria, people have a strong inclination towards enjoying and discussing various weather conditions, including warm summers, rainy summers, and snowy winters. This cultural behavior is deeply ingrained in the society and is considered a normative aspect of Bulgarian culture, with a significant portion of the sampled population embracing and valuing this practice. The appreciation for diverse weather patterns reflects the cultural significance of nature and the environment within Bulgarian society. This behavior is widely regarded as a common and integral part of the Bulgarian cultural identity.

In Bulgaria, people have a strong preference for traditional Bulgarian cuisine, which includes popular dishes such as baklava and banica, as well as a tendency to consume various parts of animals as part of their food culture. The goal of this behavior is to understand and appreciate the rich culinary heritage of Bulgaria. It is worth noting that Bulgaria, despite being a small country, is a significant exporter of wheat and other grains, which likely contributes to the prevalence of traditional food preferences. This culinary inclination is widely regarded as a normative aspect of Bulgarian culture by a significant portion of the sampled population.

In Bulgaria and Bulgarian households, it is a common practice for people, including children, to consume alcohol, including homemade liquor, from a young age. This behavior is influenced by the absence of a legal drinking age and a tradition of getting drunk, reflecting a cultural acceptance of early alcohol consumption. A significant portion of the sampled population regards this practice as normative within Bulgarian society.

In Bulgaria and the UK, people of Bulgarian cultural background are known to enjoy and frequently consume coffee, often opting for affordability and convenience through the use of vending machines or coffee machines. The cultural perception of coffee is that it is widely available and affordable, contributing to its popularity within this cultural group. This behavior is widely regarded as a normative and common practice among a significant portion of the sampled population.

In Bulgaria, particularly in Sofia and central Bulgaria, people and residents exhibit a strong preference for drinking water, including tap water, mineral water, and specific brands. This preference is influenced by concerns about the safety and taste of the water. The cultural norm emphasizes the importance of the quality and source of drinking water, with a significant portion of the sampled population sharing these concerns. The attention to water consumption reflects a common and widely regarded behavior within the Bulgarian cultural context.

In historical and international contexts, Bulgaria and its people emphasize the country's historical significance, highlighting its age and substantial contributions to history. Bulgaria is often regarded as the oldest country in Europe, boasting a rich history and cultural heritage. The emphasis on Bulgaria's historical importance is widely regarded as a normative behavior within the sampled population. This strong emphasis on historical significance reflects the pride and reverence for Bulgaria's enduring legacy, as perceived by a significant portion of the sampled population.

In Bulgarian toilets, people follow specific paper-throwing practices influenced by old customs and the diverse designs of toilets. These practices are shaped by traditional beliefs and the layout of the facilities. The sampled population generally regards these practices as a common and customary way of using the facilities. This indicates that a significant portion of the sampled population agrees that these paper-throwing practices are a normative part of the toilet culture in Bulgaria.

In Bulgaria, there is a prevalent cultural behavior among the people to engage in cost-conscious shopping, which involves purchasing inexpensive goods and comparing prices to those in Turkey. This practice is influenced by the perception that prices in Bulgaria are notably cheaper, particularly for staple items like bread and beer. As a result, a significant portion of the sampled population considers this cost-conscious shopping behavior to be a common and accepted practice within the Bulgarian cultural context.

In Bulgaria and its cuisine, it is customary for people to consider and prepare Moussaka as a traditional dish, often emphasizing its distinction from Greek and Turkish versions. This culinary practice is widely regarded as a normative behavior within the sampled population, reflecting the significance and pride attached to Bulgarian culinary heritage. The attention to differentiating their version of Moussaka showcases the cultural importance placed on preserving and celebrating their unique culinary identity.

In Bulgaria, it is common for people, including young teens, pre-teens, and teachers, to engage in smoking as a normalized and prevalent behavior, often seen on balconies. Despite some efforts to change these habits, smoking remains a widely accepted practice, with the goal of finding happiness and altering smoking behaviors. This behavior is not considered a crime and is prevalent, with Bulgaria having the highest smoking rates in Europe. Within the sampled population, a significant portion regards smoking as a normative behavior, although there are ongoing attempts to shift this cultural practice.

In Bulgarian cuisine and culture, people express a strong preference for and take great pride in Musaka, a traditional dish that is often regarded as a national symbol. This dish holds significant cultural importance and is deeply cherished by the Bulgarian population, reflecting a sense of national identity and heritage. The sampled population widely regards this behavior as normative, indicating that the majority of individuals within the Bulgarian cultural group share this strong preference and pride for Musaka.

In Bulgaria and the Balkans, both locals and tourists tend to express and prioritize safety, often perceiving the region as safer than others. The goal of this behavior is to feel secure, and this perception of safety is influenced by personal experiences and comparisons to other regions. While a significant portion of the sampled population considers safety to be a priority and views the region as relatively safe, there is also a notable portion that may not share this perception. Therefore, the prioritization of safety and the perception of the region's safety level are somewhat controversial among the sampled population.

In Bulgarian schools, both students and teachers engage in smoking despite prohibitions. Students are observed smoking in designated areas or secretly in toilets, while teachers smoke on school grounds. In response, teachers either call students' families to address the issue or choose to ignore the smoking behavior. This behavior is considered controversial and not widely accepted among the sampled population, with a significant portion expressing disapproval.

In Burgas and around the river in Bulgarian culture, it is observed that people use and drink sink water, even for survival purposes. The goal of this behavior is primarily to stay alive, indicating a reliance on this water source for basic needs. The act of using sink water, including for drinking, is considered a normative behavior by a significant portion of the sampled population. However, it is also noted to evoke a sense of cultural shock, possibly due to differing perceptions of water safety and hygiene practices. This behavior reflects a complex interplay of survival instincts and cultural adaptation within the specific geographical and cultural context.

During the summer in Bulgaria, people are accustomed to and adept at coping with extremely hot weather, often reaching temperatures as high as 40-45°C. This adaptation to such intense heat is considered a normative behavior within the sampled population. The ability to experience and adjust to such extreme temperatures is widely regarded as a common and expected part of the Bulgarian cultural experience during the summer months.

In various settings including Bulgaria, the UK, and upbringing, people of Bulgarian cultural background highly value and consume yogurt as an essential part of their tradition. Often referred to as "sour milk," yogurt holds significant cultural importance and is commonly enjoyed as a staple accompaniment to meals. This cultural practice of valuing and consuming yogurt is widely regarded as a normative behavior among a significant portion of the sampled population.

In winter, particularly in the city and mountainous regions of Bulgaria, it is common for people to adapt to and enjoy various aspects of cold weather. This includes embracing snow, enduring cold temperatures, and even taking vacations specifically to experience the cold climate. The appreciation for the winter season is deeply ingrained in the cultural practices of Bulgarians, with a significant portion of the sampled population regarding this behavior as normative. The enjoyment of cold weather and the activities associated with it are widely regarded as a standard part of the winter experience in Bulgarian culture.

Bulgarian individuals and content creators, both within and outside Bulgaria, actively engage with and promote Bulgarian culture through various platforms such as social media and videos. Their goal is to showcase and educate others about Bulgarian culture, fostering a mutual exchange of knowledge and understanding. This behavior is observed across different settings, including social media, living abroad, and watching videos, with the audience and people in the UK being the primary recipients of this cultural promotion. The sampled population perceives this engagement with Bulgarian culture as relatively common, with a significant portion agreeing that it is a normative practice within the Bulgarian cultural group.

In various social settings in Bulgaria, particularly among young people, engaging in smoking is a common and often proudly normalized behavior. This behavior is prevalent in settings such as schools, public spaces, and social gatherings. Smoking is widely regarded as a normative behavior by a significant portion of the sampled population.

In Bulgaria, amidst challenging economic conditions, the people perceive the economy as stagnant or unresponsive, despite the country having a GDP of 20,000 per capita. This outlook reflects the prevalent experience of economic struggles within the cultural context. The sampled population widely regards this perception as a common viewpoint.

In Bulgaria, it is common for people to adapt to unique and sometimes challenging sanitation practices, such as using trash for toilet paper and having limited access to garbage disposals. Despite these practices, there is a preference for real toilets and IT rooms, indicating a desire for modern amenities. This behavior is widely regarded as normative within the sampled population, reflecting a strong cultural adherence to these sanitation practices.

In Bulgarian schools, students are accustomed to adapting to shifting schedules, which may involve attending classes in shifts and changing these shifts on a monthly basis. This practice can present challenges for students as they navigate the adjustments required by the changing schedules. Despite the difficulties, around a significant portion of the sampled population agrees that this adaptive behavior is relatively common within the Bulgarian school system.

In Bulgaria, it is common for children to engage in outdoor play, emphasizing socialization and physical activity. Parents may resort to physical discipline as a means of upbringing, reflecting the traditional approach to child-rearing within the parent-child relationship. Additionally, adults in Bulgarian culture are notably cautious about children's safety, demonstrating a collective concern for their well-being. The limited availability of playgrounds and kids' menus further underscores the emphasis on outdoor play and the use of physical discipline as a normative aspect of child-rearing. This cultural behavior is widely regarded as standard by a significant portion of the sampled population in Bulgaria.

In Bulgaria, it is a common practice for both people and store owners to engage in shopping activities at all hours, with stores remaining open 24/7, including Sundays. The presence of 24/7 shops on every corner reflects the widespread availability of this shopping culture. This behavior is widely regarded as the norm within the sampled population, indicating a high level of acceptance and prevalence.

In the context of history and education within the Bulgarian and Serbian cultural groups, people prioritize and take pride in learning about their rich history. This emphasis on historical knowledge is widely regarded as a normative behavior within these cultural groups. The population sampled for this information unanimously agrees that the pursuit of understanding and cherishing their historical heritage is a common and valued practice. This dedication to historical learning reflects the deep appreciation and pride these cultural groups hold for their shared past, shaping their educational and societal values.

In Bulgaria, particularly in educational settings, students and teachers engage in education with a strong emphasis on language learning. The goal of this behavior is to effectively learn and teach, fostering a supportive teacher-student relationship. Additionally, students seek help from their peers as part of their learning process. However, this cultural behavior is perceived as disadvantaged in language learning, particularly in the context of language high schools in Burgas. Despite this perception, the sampled population widely regards this behavior as normative within Bulgarian educational settings, indicating that a significant portion of the population values and upholds the importance of language learning and effective teaching methods.

In Bulgarian culture, it is common for people to openly express and take pleasure in admiring food, often emphasizing its deliciousness. This cultural behavior is widely regarded as the norm within the sampled population. The act of openly appreciating and enjoying food is deeply ingrained in the social fabric, reflecting the high value placed on culinary experiences and the enjoyment of meals. This behavior is considered a standard and widely accepted practice among the Bulgarian cultural group.

In various locations across Bulgaria, including Sofia, Varna, and Nessebar, both locals and tourists engage in a range of activities, from visiting popular destinations to recommending places, and even yelling 'kur za levski'. These activities are aimed at having a great time, ensuring safety, and fostering new friendships. The behavior of engaging in these activities is widely regarded as a normative and standard practice within the Bulgarian cultural context, regardless of the relationship between the individuals involved. This inclusive and lively approach to socializing and exploring the country's offerings is embraced by a significant portion of the sampled population, reflecting the cultural vibrancy and openness to new experiences.

In Bulgarian culture, it is common for people to possess a wide range of items and resources, reflecting a normative behavior within the sampled population. This indicates that a significant portion of the sampled population agrees that having a diverse array of possessions is a standard practice within Bulgarian society.

Bulgarians are champions at indirect communication. One needs to observe the manner and tone of the speaker to understand fully. Many Bulgarians are direct but use non verbal communication extensively. Sometimes it is helpful to ask the same question numerous times to see if the response changes. For example, when inviting someone out the initial answer might be “no” but if asked again the response sometimes changes with a little encouragement by asking again. Bulgarians are not afraid to raise their voices. Even if they sound upset and it appears they quarreling, usually they are not and the conversation will end in a friendly manner. T he closer people are the more they may actually argue and fight but it's never taken personally.

Depending on the relationship, personal space when speaking may vary. Between family and friends there is little personal space. With members of the opposite sex and business colleagues, it is appropriate to keep and arm’s length of personal space when conversing.

Direct eye contact is fine in most situations. Looking in a person's eyes while conversing shows honesty. In communication between men and women, holding the gaze a bit longer is usually viewed as a sign of interest (goes both ways). Between men this is usually viewed as a threat or competition.

For business, punctuality is expected for meetings, arriving to the workplace and deadlines. However for social situations and engagements time is much more fluid and negotiable. Dinners in usually take at least a couple of hours, and if it is for a special occasion expect at least 4 hours of eating and drinking. When socializing Bulgarians take their time and enjoy the others’ company. For buses and trains it is hard to predict in most rural areas. Most of the bus stations have timetables for all the buses, but when the schedule was last updated is unknown. It is better to ask about the times for buses and trains. Also some bus drivers will decide to take a break and pull of the side of the road at a café and enjoy and coffee and cigarette. Right now in most urban areas, the buses have GPS systems and they tell you the ETA for the next bus. In large cities the buses schedules are fairly dense (sometimes every 3 minutes but can go up to 15-20 minutes in off hours and low traffic routes). Be aware of pickpockets in buses. All in all, transportation is becoming more reliable but don’t become angry or shocked if there are delays – it happens.

Gender roles while still mostly traditional but are beginning to change rapidly. For over 30 years the quota in universities has been 50/50 for men and women. The flight of people from the villages and small towns is also changing the traditional roles. Men are usually the workers and providers for the family and women are expected to do the cooking and cleaning. While the women play a large role in child rearing, men are also involved .

Unlike most of the world, Bulgaria has different head gestures to signify “no” and “yes.” Shaking your head from side to side indicates“yes” and an up and down movement means “no.” This is an extremely hard habit to break and very confusing for Bulgarians to understand when speaking to a foreigner. The best thing to do is keep your head still and just say “yes/da” or “no/ne.” “No” is also expressed with a sudden downward jerk of the head and a clicking sound made with the mouth. Many children use this method. Pointing is acceptable in and when beckoning someone the backwards hand wave is used, use the whole hand, not just one finger. Making a circular motion using the index finger while pointing to the side of one’s head is a rude gesture indicating that someone is crazy or deranged.

The legal drinking age is 18 but it is not heavily enforced. The legal smoking age is 18 and has a high percentage of smokers. Penalties for possession, use, or trafficking in illegal drugs in are strict, and convicted offenders can expect jail sentences and heavy fines. Foreigners charged with a crime may be denied permission to depart.

Bargaining for prices in markets or stores is not usually done. However some vendors will raise their prices for foreigners, which under EU law it is illegal for them to do. When traveling to , it is very helpful to know the Cyrillic alphabet. It is easy to learn and can be accomplished on the plane ride to . Besides Sofia , some ski resorts and the Black Sea Coast English is not commonly known. So knowing useful phrases is helpful. Especially if you have to use a taxi, have the destination written in Cyrillic or know how to pronounce it clearly.

For men : Suits are the norm. Dark colors are the way to go. For women : Standard business attire. Stylish, yet conservative. Jeans are usually not appropriate but this may vary depending on the industry one is working in.

Mr. and Mrs. are used during formal occasions and when first meeting someone, but don’t be surprised by being called by your first name. Formality wanes as time goes on. There is little protocol surround the giving and receiving of business cards.

It is best to allow for a good amount of small talk before speaking about business. Direct eye contact is a must. It is viewed as showing sincerity. Meetings can take awhile. Bulgarians tend to be detailed oriented. Remain patient. Business moves at a slower pace and paperwork is very important in business transactions. Especially when dealing with the Bulgarian government, business transactions can be hampered or stalled by bureaucracy.
Bulgarians are not afraid to raise their voices. Even if they sound upset and it appears they quarreling, usually they are not and the conversation will end in a friendly manner.

If you are asked to visit a business associates house it is expected that you bring a gift. A typical gift would be a box of chocolates, dessert of some sort, a bottle of wine or fruit. They do not have to be wrapped because the host will usually serve the gift right after it is given. Gifts to avoid include lilies and chrysanthemums (used at funerals), overly expensive/lavish gifts, and even (odd numbers are lucky) sets of gifts. Odd/Even only applies to flowers not other objects. Gifts are usually opened right away.

The school year begins September 15 th and ends in May/June. (different grades end on different days). Dress is a little more formal than universities in the USA . Students usually wear slacks or nice jeans. Grades are usually given on a 2-6 scale, with 6 being the highest and 2 being failing.

Smoking and drinking among university students is common but being excessively drunk is looked down on especially for women. Men usually ask the women out on dates and are very straight forward. A typical date might be going to a café or meyhana (cultural restaurant).
